title: On the Benefits of Weight Normalization for Overparameterized Matrix Sensing
claim: Training under this method proceeds through successive plateaus (saddles), with components learned one at a time in a staircase pattern.
layout: 6 plots in 2x3 grid, each with its own metric title below
description: A 2x3 grid of line plots from a training run over 2000 iterations. Each panel has its metric as a caption below it, with math notation in several of them. (a) Squared reconstruction error on a log scale falls in a staircase of plateaus and then drops sharply near iteration 1700. (b) Gradient norm on a log scale, with blue for X and orange for Theta, shows periodic peaks and dips at the plateaus. (c) Distance to the best rank-ρ approximation, with five colored curves for ρ=0 to 4, switches between levels as the plateaus change. (d) Singular values of Φ_t Φ_tᵀ for i=1 to 5 rise from 0 to 1 one after another, in sigmoid steps. (e) The trace of Ψ_t Ψ_tᵀ steps down from about 10 to 5. (f) Singular values of Θ_t rise in sequence to different final levels. The eye goes first to the staircase in (a) and the staggered colored sigmoids in (d) and (f).
caption: The saddle-to-saddle (i.e., sequential learning) behaviors in WN. The x-axis corresponds to the iteration number, and the y-axis follows the subfigure title. (a) Each plateau signifies a saddle; (b) gradient norm at saddles drops by orders; (c) saddles strongly relate to the best rank-ρ approximation of A; (d) sequential learning in the alignment between Xt and U; (e) sequential learning in the alignment between Xt and U⊥; and, (f) sequential pattern in the magnitude variable Θt.
abstract: While normalization techniques are widely used in deep learning, their theoretical understanding remains relatively limited. In this work, we establish the benefits of (generalized) weight normalization (WN) applied to the overparameterized matrix sensing problem. We prove that WN with Riemannian optimization achieves linear convergence, yielding an exponential speedup over standard methods that do not use WN. Our analysis further demonstrates that both iteration and sample complexity improve polynomially as the level of overparameterization increases. To the best of our knowledge, this work provides the first characterization of how WN leverages overparameterization for faster convergence in matrix sensing.
